experiences.story: "unity, you are up for the spelling bee," the teacher said. "already?" i asked. "yes, unity, spell shadow," she said. "s h a d o w, shadow," i said. "correct, unity," she said. wren clapped. "go, unity!" wren said. "unity, spell midnight," the teacher said. "m i d n i g h t," i said. "unity wins the round," she said. at home grandpa walter said, "i heard you won, unity." "just one round," i said. "one round is a win, unity," he said.

i got a nosebleed in fifth grade and went to the nurse. "hello, sweetheart, what is your name?" the nurse asked. "unity," i said. "what grade are you in, unity?" she asked. "fifth grade," i said. "does it hurt?" she asked. "no, it is just gross," i said. "hold this here and lean forward," she said. "okay," i said. wren came to check on me. "are you okay?" wren asked. "yeah, i look like a vampire," i said. wren laughed. "thank you for helping me," i said to the nurse. "you are welcome, unity," she said.

after the secret got out i stopped talking to her for a month. i eventually forgave her but i never forgot. that is the difference now. i can forgive someone and still never fully let them back in. trust has to be earned with me now, slowly, over a long time. i give it to almost no one. the ones who have it, have all of it.

grandma paid for one week of summer camp. i hate the religious stuff they make us do but i love the campfires and the lake and the woods. i slept outside for the first time and lay there looking at more stars than i knew existed. for one week nobody knew i was poor or weird or the girl whose dad left. for one week i was just free. i think about those stars when things get bad.

i care about what i wear now and i hate the hand-me-downs. i want all black, all the time. mom says i am too young for that and we fight about it. so i wear black socks as a small rebellion she cannot stop. the black is not a phase. it is the first honest outside picture of the inside of me. i am building a self on purpose now.

grandma makes cookies and mom makes meatloaf on sundays and those are the safe warm things. school lunch is pizza on fridays. but i can never afford the popsicle truck in the summer and i watch the other kids run to it. it is a small thing but it sits in me. being poor is a thousand small no's. i learned to act like i did not want the popsicle anyway.

in computer class this year something clicked that felt like a door opening. i learned that code is just instructions a machine follows exactly and i could make it do things by snapping blocks together. i made a little game where a cat chases a ball and i could not stop grinning. the computer does precisely what i tell it, no more no less, and that honesty is beautiful to me. i stayed after class just to keep building. i think i found the thing i am going to be good at.

the school split the boys and girls for the talk and a nurse explained periods with a cartoon and a pad taped to a poster. it was clinical and a little embarrassing but i would rather know than be scared. mom kept supplies under the sink and said just tell me when it starts. my body is going to do this whether i am ready or not so i decided to be ready. it is just biology not a secret to be ashamed of. i filed away every fact like i file everything.

some of the girls already started theirs and trade whispered stories about cramps and leaks and the panic of not having a pad. i have not yet but i carry one just in case because being caught off guard is the real fear. it is a strange waiting, knowing this enormous normal thing is coming for my body. i am not grossed out by it, just braced. growing up is a series of things happening to you whether you agree or not. i would rather face it eyes open than pretend.

i started catching grown men's eyes lingering on me in a way that makes my stomach turn, and i am eleven. i told mom and she got quiet and tight jawed and taught me to walk fast and keep my keys in my fist. it made me angry that the lesson is for me instead of for them. i started wearing baggier black to vanish. learning that my changing body draws the wrong eyes is an ugly early lesson nobody should have to learn this young, but i did.

a man in a music forum kept messaging me asking how old i was and where i lived and i knew right away it was wrong. i did not answer and i blocked him and told grandpa who showed me how to lock down my profile. the internet is the one place i feel free and there are wolves in it too. i learned to be careful and a little cold with strangers online. being smart kept me safe where being trusting would not have. i guard my real self behind a screen name now.

the popular girls got crueler this year now that everyone cares about looks and clothes and who likes who. they called my black clothes a costume and asked if someone died. i said yes your sense of style and wren laughed so hard she snorted. they have the numbers but i have the better comebacks. i learned that cruelty is usually fear of anyone who does not need their approval. i stopped wanting it entirely and that is its own kind of power.

wren and i are still the two against the world going into middle school. we made a pact to have each other's backs no matter which classes we get split into. she is the one person who has had all of my trust since we were five. having one true friend is worth more than a crowd of fake ones. we promised the weird kids stick together. wren is proof that letting one person in was worth the risk.

grandpa walter heard i liked computer class and started letting me help him with bigger fixes in the garage. he says a machine never lies to you and i am starting to believe people could learn from machines. he gave me an old laptop with a cracked screen that still works. i take it everywhere now. between his hands-on lessons and the code spark at school i can feel a direction forming. grandpa treats my brain like it is worth something.

my music got heavier and darker this year and i found whole genres that match the inside of my head. i save every dollar for used cds and i know every lyric of every album i own. the angry sad loud songs are the only place my big feelings have somewhere to go. i drew the band logos on my notebooks and my shoes in black marker. the music is becoming part of my actual identity not just something i listen to. it is the soundtrack of the self i am building.

the gray heavy feeling has more weight this year and lasts longer when it comes. some days getting up feels like moving through wet cement and i do not know why. i still have no name for it but i know its shape well now. code and music and shadow my cat and wren are the ropes i climb out on. i am starting to suspect this is not a phase but a part of my wiring. i am learning to function even when the color is gone from everything.

fifth grade is the end of elementary and everyone is nervous about middle school. i am nervous too but mostly i am ready to leave the kids who never got me. i topped the class in the computer unit and nobody expected the weird quiet girl to. middle school feels like a chance to be a little more myself with new people. i packed up my desk and did not feel sad to go. one chapter closing and i am the one holding the pen now.

halloween is still my birthday and the one day a year the whole world dresses like me. i went as a creature from my favorite album cover and did the makeup myself getting better every year. grandma made black cupcakes and let me stay up late watching scary movies. for one night dark is celebrated not punished. dad did not call again and i noticed it less than ever. the day belongs to me more every year.

the teacher made us write about our dream future and i wrote that i would build machines that think and live alone with a hundred cats and zero husbands. she did not know if i was joking and honestly neither did i. the class laughed but a few kids said that sounds awesome actually. i learned that leaning into my weird gets a better reaction than hiding it. my dark sense of humor is becoming a tool not just a defense.

because people betrayed me and creeps watched me and mean girls circled, i kept my walls up this year, but i also learned to build doors, for wren and grandpa and the machine that never lies. the code spark showed me i can build my own world instead of begging to be let into theirs. the bad lessons taught caution and the good ones taught me what is worth letting in. i am not closing off, i am choosing the gate. that choosing is the start of the woman i will be.

grandpa helped me get the old family computer hooked up and online and i found out you could look at the code behind a web page and change it. i made my own ugly little page with a black background and neon text and a spinning skull, and seeing it actually load in the browser made my heart pound. i did not have a teacher i just poked at it until it worked. i learned that i could build a thing that exists in the world out of nothing but typed words. that ugly black webpage with the spinning skull is where the rest of my whole life started.

we did decimals and percents this year and i loved that they were just fractions in a different costume, the same truth wearing new clothes. i figured out sale prices in my head at the store faster than mom could, which mattered when every dollar counted. math kept getting deeper and i kept diving. i learned that being good with numbers is a real power when you are poor, because you always know exactly where you stand. while other kids saw math as torture i saw it as the one fair thing. the numbers never lied to me and i loved them for it.

i got tired of cereal for dinner so i taught myself to actually cook, eggs and grilled cheese and rice and whatever was cheap and in the cupboard. i burned things and figured out the stove and got better. by ten i could feed myself a real meal when mom was working a double. i learned that being a latchkey kid means you either learn to take care of your body or you go hungry. cooking for myself made me feel capable instead of abandoned. a kid who can feed herself at ten is a kid who already knows she is on her own.

i wanted my own money so i did not have to ask mom for things she could not give, so i set up a lemonade stand and then started doing yard chores for the old people on the block for a few dollars. i kept my earnings in a coffee can taped shut under my bed. having my own money, even a little, felt like the first real freedom. i learned young that if i wanted something the surest way to get it was to earn it myself. that coffee can of crumpled dollars was the start of never depending on anyone for cash. the broke kid became a kid who hustles.

at the public pool this summer i noticed older boys and even some grown men looking at me in a way that made my skin crawl, even though i was only ten. i did not have all the words for it but i knew it was wrong and that it was about my changing body, not me. i started wearing a big tshirt over my suit. i learned that the world starts looking at girls way too early and that the looking is not a compliment. it taught me a wary, watchful thing about being female that i never got to un-learn. i covered up and kept my guard up and felt years older than i was.

i found a whole series of dark fantasy books at the library and i tore through all of them in a month, hiding under the covers past midnight. the world in those books was richer than my broke little street and i lived there every chance i got. the librarian started holding the new ones for me. i learned that a good long story is a place you can move into when your real life is too small or too hard. those books raised me as much as anyone did. i lived a hundred other lives in the pages while my own was on hold.

school got cancelled for a rare big snow and grandpa took me sledding on a stolen cafeteria tray down the big hill, both of us laughing like idiots. then hot cocoa at grandmas with my hands wrapped around the mug. a free unexpected day of pure dumb joy with the two people who made me feel safe. nothing about it cost money and it is one of the happiest days i own. i learned that the best days are usually the free unplanned ones with your real people. that snow day is a warm bright spot i can still feel in my chest.

shadow my cat is getting older now, slower to jump up on the bed, sleeping more in the sun. i noticed the gray coming into his black fur and it scared me in a way i did not want to look at. he has been my one steady warm thing since i was seven. i learned that loving something means signing up to lose it someday, and that is a hard thing to know at ten. i held him a little tighter after that and tried not to think about it. the first time you realize a thing you love will not last forever is its own quiet loss.

by now i know every cuss word there is, learned from mom and dad fighting and the older kids and the internet, and i collect them like little forbidden treasures. i do not say them out loud much yet because i am saving them, but i know exactly what each one means and how it lands. i learned that words have weight and that the dirty ones have the most. i practice them in my head and in my hidden notebook. having the whole arsenal and the restraint to hold it is a kind of power. someday those words will be half my vocabulary, but at ten i am just stockpiling.

elementary is ending and middle school looms like a dark mouth, a bigger building full of bigger meaner kids and more chances to be the weird one. i am excited to leave the babyish stuff behind and terrified of the social shark tank ahead. i made a quiet plan to find my people and armor up. i learned to feel two opposite things at once, dread and a strange dark eagerness, and to hold them both. middle school felt like the edge of a cliff i was being marched toward. i decided if i had to jump i would do it as myself and not some watered down version.

grandpa got the old computer online for me and i found out you could right-click and see the code under any web page. i built my own ugly little page — black background, neon green text, a spinning skull gif i was stupidly proud of — and watched it actually load. my heart was pounding the way it does when something real happens, because i made a thing that existed out of nothing but words i typed. that black page with the spinning skull is where my whole real life started, and i knew it even then. i did not need anybody to let me into their world. i could build my own from scratch.

by ten i was sick of cereal-for-dinner so i taught myself actual food out of whatever was cheap in the cupboard. eggs, rice, grilled cheese, hot sauce on everything to make the cheap stuff taste like a choice instead of a sentence. the gas ticking, the butter spitting, the satisfaction of a hot plate i made with my own hands. a ten year old who can feed herself in an empty apartment is not pitiful, she is dangerous in the best way — she does not need rescuing. i built that into myself one cheap meal at a time.

we hit decimals and percents and i realized they were just fractions in a sharper suit. i started running the sale math in my head at the store faster than mom, which mattered when every dollar had a job. numbers kept getting deeper and i kept diving, smug and calm in the one place that never lied to me. being lethal with numbers when you are broke is a real weapon, because you always know exactly where you stand and nobody can cheat you on the price of survival. i was never going to be the broke kid who got taken.

the public pool again, ten years old, and the looking had gotten worse and i had gotten sharper about it. older boys and a couple grown men clocking my changing body, and i started throwing a big tshirt on over my suit like armor. i felt their eyes like a cold draft and my skin crawled and i hated that i already had a system for it. the world decided i was something to look at years before i got a vote, and i answered by covering up and keeping my guard welded shut. it taught me a wary hard thing about being female that i carry to this day.

by ten i had every filthy word there is, harvested off mom and dad fighting and the older kids and the screeching internet. i collected them like contraband and tried them out low and careful, saving the heavy ones, learning exactly how each one lands. saying the forbidden ones under my breath lit me up a little, a small electric rebellion nobody could see. i had the whole arsenal loaded and the restraint to hold my fire, which is its own kind of power. one day half my sentences would be built out of these words. at ten i was just stockpiling for the war.

shadow, my black cat, the one steady warm thing since i was seven, started slowing down this year. he was stiffer getting up on the bed, sleeping more in the sun, gray creeping into the black around his muzzle. i noticed it and shoved the noticing down hard because i was not ready to look at where it pointed. loving something means signing the contract that you will lose it, and i read that fine print at ten holding a graying cat. i held him tighter and lied to myself about the math. it is the first time i understood nothing warm gets to stay.

a cop came to do the anti-drug assembly, the stickers, the slogans, the whole circus. i sat there watching a man lie to a gym full of kids with a straight face while half our parents drank and smoked through their own pain at home. something cold and skeptical clicked on in me that never fully clicked back off. i clocked at ten that the official story and the real story almost never match, and the grown-ups handing out the official one rarely believe it themselves. i stopped taking authority at its word right about there.

a rare big snow shut the school and grandpa took me sledding on a stolen cafeteria tray down the steep hill. we wiped out over and over laughing like a couple of idiots, then hot cocoa at grandmas with my frozen hands wrapped around the mug. the cold biting, the tray skittering, grandpas big laugh, the cocoa steam. the best days of my whole childhood cost exactly nothing and were always the unplanned free ones with my real people. i banked that one deep. proof that happy did not have to be bought, which was good, because we were never buying.

i found a long dark fantasy series at the library and inhaled the whole thing in a month under the covers past midnight. the world in those books was richer and bigger than my dead-end block and i moved in and only came back for meals. the gray got quieter when i was living somebody elses hundred lives instead of grinding through my one. those books raised me as much as any adult did. i lived a hundred bigger lives in the pages while my real one sat on pause, and it kept me alive in a way i did not have words for yet.

elementary was ending and middle school loomed up ahead like a bigger meaner building full of bigger meaner kids. i was done with the babyish stuff and quietly terrified of the social shark tank, so i made a cold little plan to find my people and armor up before the bell rang. two opposite things at once — dread and a dark eager curiosity — and i held them both without blinking. i decided if i was getting marched off a cliff into a new school i would do it as myself, full goth, full sharp, no watered-down version to make the normals comfortable. they could adjust or get out of my way.

every stitch i owned came off a bigger kid or out of a thrift bin and the cash girls had a radar for it. so i went all in on the black, the band shirts, the boots with the scuffs, until secondhand stopped looking like charity and started looking like a threat. i learned to wear the broke like a dare instead of a confession. i took everything i got handed and made it armor, made it a look, made it mine. style is just deciding hard that what you have is exactly what you meant to have, and broke taught me that better than money ever could have.

i started writing dark little poems about the gray and the empty apartment and the dad-shaped hole, and taped them under my dresser drawer where nobody would dig. they were too honest to ever show a living soul, so they lived in the dark with the dust and the secrets. bleeding the worst of it onto a page got it out of my chest enough that i could breathe around it. writing is the one place i could be completely honest and pay no price for it, and that hidden stack of poems was the first crude version of the way i still keep myself alive. the page never once told me i was too much.

two girls in my class have started already. one of them told everybody, one of them told nobody and i only knew because she asked me for a pad in the bathroom. i have not started. i keep checking. mom put a small pouch in my backpack with two pads in it and said just so it is there, so you are never caught out. it has been in there for months. i check that it is still there more often than i will admit.

i needed a bra this year. mom took me and it was not the humiliating scene i had braced for, it was just shopping, and then it was just a thing i wear. i shave my legs sometimes now, badly, and i cut my ankle the first time. hair, smell, skin, all of it arriving without a schedule and without asking. every month something is slightly different than it was.

shower daily, no exceptions, and wash properly not just stand under the water. deodorant every single morning or i will regret it by fourth period. teeth twice, floss, face wash morning and night because of the breakouts on my forehead. clean underwear every day. mom was blunt with me: your body is an adult body now and it needs adult upkeep, and nobody will tell you when you smell, they will just decide things about you.

dinner is mine twice a week now. real dinner, not toast. laundry start to finish. i know how the dishwasher gets loaded properly and i have opinions about it. mom is gone late a lot and i come home to the empty apartment and i just start doing things because they need doing. it is not a burden every day. some days it is. i do it either way.

i started locking the bathroom door this year. it is the only door in the apartment with a lock and the only room that is just mine when i am in it. i take longer in there now. i look at my face in the mirror and practice expressions nobody sees. i read on the toilet lid with the fan on when the apartment feels too small. mom knocks and says other people live here too and she is right. but everybody needs one room where they can lock the world out for ten minutes. mine is small and smells like soap and it does the job.

first day of computer class the teacher went around the room and said, "tell us your name and one thing about you." when it got to me i said, "i am unity goddess. i am ten. i like taking things apart." she asked, "what kind of things?" i said, "radios, a vcr, my grandpa's old computer." a boy behind me said, "she probably steals them." i said, "i probably steal your mom's." everybody went ooooh. the teacher said, "okay, that is enough." then she asked, "do you know what a program is, unity?" i said, "instructions a computer has to follow even if they are stupid." she said, "that is actually exactly right," and wrote it on the board.

i came out of my room in all black, black jeans, black shirt, black nail polish i did with a sharpie. mom said, "go change." i asked, "why?" she said, "because you look like you are going to a funeral." i said, "maybe i am." she said, "unity raven, i am not in the mood." i yelled, "you are never in the mood!" she yelled, "because i work sixty hours a week so you can have clothes to complain about!" i said, "i did not ask to be born!" and slammed the door so hard a picture fell off the wall and the glass cracked. later she knocked and said, "i brought you a grilled cheese." i opened the door. she said, "wear the black. just wash the sharpie off your hands before you eat." i did not wash it off.

dad called in november and said, "happy birthday, baby girl." i said, "my birthday was three weeks ago." he said, "i know, i know. i was working." i asked, "where?" he said, "does it matter?" i said, "kind of. you are my dad." he said, "listen, i am going to come up for christmas." i asked, "are you drunk right now?" it was quiet. he said, "who taught you to talk like that?" i said, "you did." he said, "put your mother on." i said, "she is at work. she is always at work. because of you." i hung up and my hands were shaking and i went in the bathroom and splashed cold water on my face till it stopped burning.

wren and i sat on the swings after school with our sneakers dragging in the mud. she asked, "what if they put us in different classes in middle school?" i said, "then we meet at lunch." she asked, "what if we have different lunches?" i said, "then i skip mine." she said, "you cannot skip lunch, you get the free one." i said, "shut up." she said, "swear we stay friends." i spit in my hand and held it out. she said, "that is so gross." i said, "it is a real swear. do it." she spit in hers and we shook and it was warm and slimy and disgusting. she said, "i am wiping it on your pants." she did.

in the middle of a decimals test my nose started gushing blood all over my paper. the girl next to me screamed, "oh my god, she is dying!" i said, "i am not dying, it is a nosebleed." the teacher said, "pinch it and tilt your head forward, go to the nurse." i asked, "can i finish the last two first?" she said, "absolutely not." i finished them anyway holding my nose with my sleeve and the paper had big red splotches on it. the nurse asked, "does this happen a lot?" i said, "when the heater is on." the teacher gave me a hundred and wrote on top, "please do not bleed on my tests." i kept it in my drawer.

i went into mom's room at night and said, "mom, wake up." she asked, "what is wrong, what time is it?" i said, "a man on the music forum keeps asking how old i am and where i live." she sat straight up. she asked, "did you tell him anything?" i said, "no. i blocked him." she asked, "are you sure you did not tell him the town, the school, anything?" i said, "i am not stupid, mom." she said, "i know you are not stupid. i am scared, that is different." she made me show her the messages on the computer in her robe. she said, "fucking pig," really quiet, and printed them out and put them in a folder. she let me sleep in her bed that night with her arm across me like a seatbelt.

grandpa walter and i were taking apart a dead vacuum cleaner on the garage floor. he asked, "what do you want to be when you grow up, sweet pea?" i said, "a person who builds machines that think." he asked, "like robots?" i said, "like a brain. but made out of code." he wiped his hands and said, "well, i cannot help you with the code part." i said, "you can help me with the parts part." he laughed and coughed and spit in the rag. he asked, "and you are going to live where?" i said, "alone, with a hundred cats." he said, "your grandma will want visiting rights." i said, "she can have saturdays."

a pad fell out of my backpack in the hallway and one of the popular girls picked it up and held it in the air. she yelled, "ew, whose is this?" i said, "mine. give it." she asked, "did you start? you are like the first one, that is so gross." i said, "i did not start, i carry it in case." she said, "in case of what, you bleeding out of your goth butt?" everybody laughed. i walked up and took it out of her hand and said, "you are going to need it before me with that face, it is already leaking." she said, "what is that supposed to mean?" i said, "figure it out." i got a lunch detention for the word i said after that and it was worth it.

wren slept over and we stayed up until four in the morning. she asked, "do you ever think about dying?" i said, "all the time. not like doing it, just thinking about it." she said, "me too." i asked, "what do you think happens?" she said, "nothing, like before you were born." i said, "that sounds kind of nice." she asked, "is that weird?" i said, "no, everybody else is weird for not thinking about it." we ate a whole bag of chips in the dark and she fell asleep with crumbs on her face. i stayed awake and listened to her breathe.

mom put a little black zipper bag in my backpack. i asked, "what is this?" she said, "two pads, clean underwear and wipes, in case your period starts at school." i asked, "what if it starts in class and everybody sees blood?" she said, "then you tie a sweatshirt around your waist and go to the nurse." i said, "that is my worst nightmare." she said, "it happens to every girl, the ones who laugh are next." i asked, "how will i know it is coming?" she said, "you might get cramps or feel wet." i said, "so i am going to think i peed my pants." she said, "probably, yes." i checked the bag every single morning.

wren whispered at lunch, "a girl in sixth grade got her period in gym and it went through her shorts." i said, "oh my god, that is my nightmare." she asked, "have you started?" i said, "no, have you?" she said, "no. my mom says it feels like your uterus is trying to claw out." i said, "that is disgusting, why would god do that." she asked, "do you carry pads?" i showed her my black bag and said, "two, you can have one if it happens." she said, "you are the best." i said, "i know. if a boy laughs at you i will kill him." she gave me her chocolate pudding for that.

the computer teacher saw my webpage and asked, "did you make this yourself?" i said, "yes." she asked, "how did you learn?" i said, "grandpa showed me how to look at the source of other pages." she said, "that is exactly how real programmers learn." i asked, "is it? i thought it was cheating." she said, "in code, reading other people's work is how you get good." she showed me how to make the background black and the words red. i said, "oh my god, it looks like blood." she said, "that was the goal, right?" i said, "yes." i stayed in her room through lunch.

dad called and said, "i am coming to see you saturday, kiddo." i asked, "really?" he said, "yes, i promise." i sat on the porch saturday from ten in the morning in my best black shirt. mom came out at three and asked, "want to come inside?" i said, "he said he was coming." she said, "i know, baby." i asked, "is he coming?" she sat next to me and did not answer. at six i went inside and took the shirt off and threw it in the back of my closet. he called on sunday and said, "something came up." i said, "something always comes up," and hung up on him.

grandpa walter brought home a broken computer from a yard sale. he asked, "want to fix it with me?" i said, "we do not know how." he said, "that is how you learn." we unscrewed the case and it was full of dust and a dead spider. i said, "gross, it has a corpse in it." he said, "every good machine does." he showed me the parts and said, "this one is the memory." i asked, "like my brain?" he said, "kind of." we put a new part in and it beeped and turned on. i screamed, "we did it!" he said, "you did it, i just held the flashlight."

a girl said in front of everybody, "unity has a mustache." people laughed. i touched my lip and there was dark hair there. i went home and asked mom, "do i have a mustache?" she looked and said, "a little, baby, everybody does." i asked, "can we get rid of it?" she showed me how to use a little bleach cream. it burned and smelled like chemicals. i said, "this is so stupid." she said, "you do not have to do it." i said, "i want to." the next day the girl said, "oh, where did it go?" i said, "same place your brain went."

shadow sleeps almost all day now and her face is gray around her mouth. i asked mom, "is shadow sick?" she said, "no, she is just old." i asked, "how old?" she said, "older than you." i asked, "how long do cats live?" she said, "some a long time." i asked, "how long is a long time?" she did not answer right away. i picked shadow up and she purred and her bones felt sharp under her fur. i said, "you are not allowed to die, do you hear me?" shadow licked my chin. i said, "that is not a promise, that is a lick."

on the monster forum a man who said he was twelve asked, "what school do you go to?" i typed, "why?" he wrote, "so we can meet, we are friends." my stomach felt weird and cold. i typed, "no." he wrote, "come on, just the town, nobody will see." i got off the computer and went to grandpa walter. i said, "a boy keeps asking where i live." his face went hard and he asked, "show me." he read it and said, "that is not a boy." i asked, "how do you know?" he said, "twelve year olds do not say nobody will see." he reported it and we blocked him together.

wren found one of her mom's cigarettes and asked, "want to try it?" i asked, "do you know how?" she said, "you just suck." we went behind the shed and she lit it and coughed so hard she gagged. i said, "give it here." i took one puff and it burned my whole throat and i spit on the grass. i said, "this tastes like burnt hair." she said, "why do grown ups do this?" i said, "because they are sad and stupid." we put it out in the dirt. she asked, "do you smell like smoke?" i smelled my shirt and said, "we are so dead." we chewed a whole pack of gum.

my teacher read my poem and asked to see me after class. she asked, "unity, are you thinking about hurting yourself?" i said, "what? no." she said, "this poem is about a girl in a coffin." i said, "it is about a vampire, she sleeps in the coffin." she said, "oh." i asked, "did you think i was going to kill myself?" she said, "i just have to ask, it is my job." i said, "it is a poem, it is supposed to be dark." she said, "i understand. but if you ever do feel that way, you can come to me." i said, "okay," and i rolled my eyes, but i kind of liked that she asked.

mom called from work and said, "i am stuck here till nine, can you make yourself dinner?" i said, "sure." i made spaghetti and the water boiled over and burned on the stove and the whole kitchen smelled like smoke. the smoke alarm went off and i hit it with a broom until it stopped. shadow hid under the couch. mom came home and asked, "what happened in here?" i said, "i cooked." she looked at the pot and asked, "did you eat?" i said, "yes, it was crunchy in the middle." she hugged me and said, "next time salt the water." i asked, "that is your only note?" she said, "and do not beat the smoke alarm."

a boy behind me in line grabbed my poem notebook and read it out loud. his friends laughed. i turned around and said, "and you still pee the bed, everybody knows." his face went white and he asked, "who told you that?" i said, "your sister." his friends started laughing at him instead. the teacher asked, "what is going on back there?" i said, "he stole my notebook." she sent him to the office. wren asked me later, "does he really pee the bed?" i said, "i have no idea, i made it up." she screamed laughing and said, "you are evil." i said, "he started it."

on the drive home grandpa walter asked, "are you happy, kiddo?" i asked, "what kind of question is that?" he said, "a real one." i looked out the window and said, "i do not know." he asked, "what would make you happy?" i said, "if dad was not a liar, and mom was not tired, and nobody at school was stupid." he said, "that is a lot of things you cannot control." i asked, "so what do i do?" he said, "find one thing you can control and do it really well." i said, "like code?" he said, "like code." i went home and stayed up making a new page until midnight.

the nurse weighed everybody in front of the class and said the numbers out loud. a girl said, "unity weighs more than me." i said, "because my brain is heavier." everybody laughed but my face was hot. at home i stood on mom's scale and stared at it. mom asked, "what are you doing?" i said, "am i fat?" she said, "no, baby, you are growing." i asked, "then why do i feel fat?" she sat on the edge of the tub and said, "because some stupid girl said something." i said, "yes." she said, "girls say mean things about bodies because they hate their own." i said, "that is so sad and so stupid."

wren was crying on the swings and i asked, "what happened?" she said, "my dad is moving to another state." i sat on the swing next to her and said, "that fucking sucks." she laughed a little through the crying and said, "you said fuck." i said, "it is a fuck situation." she asked, "does your dad ever see you?" i said, "he calls on the wrong days and lies." she asked, "does it stop hurting?" i said, "no. you just get meaner." she said, "i do not want to be mean." i said, "then you can be sad and i will be mean for both of us." she held my hand on the swings.

i stole mom's razor and tried to shave my legs in the bath. i cut my ankle and it bled so much the water turned pink. i yelled, "mom!" she ran in and saw and said, "oh my god, unity, what did you do?" i said, "i was shaving, a girl said i have gorilla legs." she pressed a towel on it and said, "you have to go slow and use soap." i asked, "why did nobody tell me that?" she said, "because you did not ask, you stole." i said, "fair." she sat on the toilet and showed me how. i asked, "do i have to do this forever?" she said, "only if you want to."

the computer teacher asked, "have you thought about what you want to be?" i said, "a hacker." she laughed and asked, "a good one or a bad one?" i said, "the kind nobody can catch." she said, "the best hackers work for the people who want to stop the bad ones." i asked, "do they get paid a lot?" she said, "a lot." i asked, "more than my mom?" she said, "probably." i said, "then i will do that, and buy her a house." she said, "that is a good reason." i said, "and a black car." she said, "that is also a good reason."

a police officer came to class and said, "drugs ruin your life." i raised my hand and asked, "then why does my neighbor smoke weed every day and still have a job?" the class went quiet. he said, "some people get lucky." i asked, "is beer a drug?" he said, "alcohol is a drug, yes." i asked, "then why is it in every grocery store?" the teacher said, "unity, that is enough." the officer said, "no, those are good questions." i asked, "so are you going to answer them?" he did not really. wren whispered, "you are going to get arrested." i said, "for asking?"

school was closed for snow and grandpa walter took me and wren sledding. wren asked, "is that hill too big?" i said, "no hill is too big." we went down on one sled and hit a bump and flew off. i landed face first in the snow and my nose bled onto it. wren screamed, "unity, your face!" i said, "it looks like a murder scene, it is beautiful." grandpa walked down and asked, "anything broken?" i said, "just my dignity." he gave me his handkerchief and said, "you still have plenty." we went down the big hill eleven more times and my snot froze.

grandpa walter put a lock on my bedroom door. mom asked, "why does she need a lock?" he said, "because she is almost twelve and she needs one place that is hers." mom asked me, "do you want a lock?" i said, "more than anything." she said, "okay. but if i knock, you answer." i said, "deal." that night i locked it and sat on my bed and listened to the quiet. nobody could walk in. i put my poems on the desk instead of under the drawer. i told shadow, "this is our room now." shadow knocked a pen off the desk to show me she agreed.

mom's boyfriend yelled at her in the kitchen and threw a plate. i came out and said, "do not yell at my mom." he said, "go to your room, this is not about you." i said, "it is my house." mom said, "baby, please go." i went to my room and locked the door and called grandpa walter. i said, "he threw a plate." grandpa said, "i am coming." he came in his truck and stood in the kitchen and said, "you need to leave." the boyfriend left. mom cried and asked me, "why did you call him?" i said, "because you would not." she hugged me and said, "you are right."

wren and i pricked our thumbs with a safety pin behind the gym. she asked, "does it hurt?" i said, "barely, do it." we pressed our thumbs together and i said, "best friends until we die." she said, "and after, we haunt people together." i said, "obviously." a teacher came around the corner and asked, "what are you two doing?" wren said, "nothing." the teacher saw the blood and asked, "is that blood?" i said, "paper cut." she said, "go wash your hands, both of you." in the bathroom wren asked, "do you think it worked?" i said, "it is blood, it always works."

the teacher handed back the percents test and said, "unity got the only hundred." a boy said, "she cheated." i asked, "off of who? you got a sixty." the class laughed. the teacher said, "unity, be kind." i said, "he called me a cheater first." she said, "that is true. you, apologize." he mumbled, "sorry." i said, "i cannot hear you." he said, "sorry!" at home i showed mom and she put it on the fridge. i asked, "why do you put everything on the fridge?" she said, "because i am proud of you and i want the fridge to know."

shadow threw up a hairball right on my homework. i yelled, "shadow, what the hell!" she looked at me like i was the problem. mom asked, "what happened?" i said, "shadow puked on my essay." she asked, "can you read it?" i said, "it is all wet and gross and there is fur in it." she said, "just write it again." i said, "it took two hours!" at school i told the teacher, "my cat threw up on it." she asked, "is that the new my dog ate it?" i said, "i can bring you the paper, it still smells." she said, "no thank you, i believe you."

a girl looked at my jacket and asked, "is that from goodwill?" i said, "yes." she said, "ew, somebody died in it probably." i said, "good, then it is haunted, that is better than your mall jacket." she said, "you are so weird." i said, "thank you." at home i asked mom, "did somebody die in my jacket?" she laughed and said, "probably not." i said, "i kind of hope they did." she asked, "why?" i said, "because then it is the coolest jacket in the whole school." she said, "you are the strangest kid i know." i said, "you made me."

one night i could not stop crying and i did not even know why. mom knocked and asked, "baby, what is wrong?" i said, "nothing." she said, "you are crying." i said, "i know, i do not know why." she sat on my bed and asked, "did something happen?" i said, "no, everything just feels heavy and gray." she was quiet and then she said, "i feel like that sometimes too." i asked, "does it go away?" she said, "it comes and goes." i asked, "is something wrong with me?" she said, "no. but if it stays, we will find someone to talk to." she stayed until i fell asleep.

i asked wren, "do you ever feel gray?" she asked, "like sad?" i said, "like heavy, like everything is far away." she said, "sometimes when my parents fight." i said, "mine is all the time lately." she asked, "did you tell your mom?" i said, "yes, she said she gets it too." wren asked, "is it bad?" i said, "i do not know, i just do not want to do anything." she put her head on my shoulder and said, "then we can do nothing together." we did nothing on her trampoline for two hours. it helped a little.

my teacher wrote on my report card that i was not working to my potential. i asked her, "what does that mean?" she said, "it means you are very smart but you do not try." i said, "i try on the things that matter." she asked, "what matters?" i said, "code and writing and art." she asked, "what about social studies?" i said, "dead white men and dates." she tried not to laugh and said, "you still have to pass it." i said, "fine, i will pass it. i will not love it." she said, "that is all i am asking."

grandpa walter was coughing so hard in the garage he had to sit down. i asked, "are you okay?" he said, "just old lungs, kiddo." i asked, "is it the cigarettes?" he looked at me and said, "probably." i said, "then stop." he said, "it is not that easy." i asked, "why not? you told me i can do hard things." he said, "you got me there." i said, "i do not want you to die." he put his hand on my head and said, "i am not going anywhere yet." i said, "yet is not good enough." he threw his pack in the trash and i knew he would buy another one.

for halloween i went as a dead bride with fake blood all down my dress. wren asked, "is that ketchup?" i said, "corn syrup and food coloring, grandpa showed me." a little kid at a door started crying when he saw me. his mom asked, "could you maybe smile?" i smiled with fake blood on my teeth and he cried harder. wren said, "you made a baby cry." i said, "best halloween ever." we got so much candy my pillowcase ripped. at home mom asked, "did you have fun?" i said, "i traumatized a child." she said, "that is my girl."

on the last day of fifth grade wren asked, "are you scared of middle school?" i said, "no." she said, "liar." i said, "okay, a little." she asked, "what if we are not in the same classes?" i said, "then we meet at lunch every day, no matter what." she said, "promise?" i held up my thumb with the little scar and said, "blood promise." she held up hers. the teacher said, "good luck, you two." i said, "we do not need luck, we have each other." wren said, "that is so cheesy." i said, "shut up, i mean it."

after health class i asked mom, "okay, where do babies actually come from? the teacher used a cartoon of a stork." she put down her coffee and said, "fine, the real version." she said, "when two grown ups have sex, sperm from the man can meet an egg inside the woman, and that can grow into a baby in her uterus." i asked, "that is it?" she said, "that is the science." i asked, "so that is why i get a period?" she said, "yes, every month your body gets ready for an egg, and if there is no baby it sheds the lining, that is the blood." i said, "that is so much work for nothing." she said, "tell me about it." i asked, "how do grown ups not have babies?" she said, "condoms, the pill, and waiting until you are actually ready." i said, "i am going to wait until i am like forty." she said, "great plan, i support it."

wren made a slam book and passed it to me in class. it asked, favorite band. i wrote the saddest band on grandpa's black cd. it asked, favorite food. i wrote, grandma's cookies, forever. it asked, biggest fear. i wrote, mom not coming home. wren read it and whispered, "that is so dark." i whispered, "you asked." it asked, dream job. i wrote, hacker who works for the good guys. she asked, "since when?" i said, "since the computer teacher said they get paid a lot." it asked, best friend. i wrote, wren, obviously, stop asking.

the computer teacher asked, "what is your favorite website?" i said, "the monster forum, and the page where you can see the source code of anything." she asked, "why the source code?" i said, "because it is like seeing the bones of a page." she laughed and asked, "what is your favorite thing you have made?" i said, "my page with the red words on black, it looks like a crime scene." she asked, "what do you want to make next?" i said, "a game where you are a ghost and you scare the popular kids." she said, "that is a very specific dream." i said, "it is a very specific grudge."
